item.title: Two-Sided Amortized Resource Analysis: Verifying Resource Lower Bounds via Ill-Typing
item.description: arXiv:2611.12925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a two-sided type system with potential for verifying resource lower bounds of functional programs. Automatic amortized resource analysis (AARA) verifies upper bounds: types carry potential, and typing certifies sufficient resources. A lower bound, however, is a necessity statement---the program evaluates only if enough resources are available---and prior type-based approaches obtain it by switching the substructural discipline of potential, so that upper and lower bounds live in separate type systems. Matching upper and lower bounds characterize a program's cost exactly. Our system combines AARA-style potential with the two-sided type systems of Ramsay and Walpole, whose central guarantee is that ill-typed programs do not evaluate. Typing formulas may constrain arbitrary terms and appear on both sides of the turnstile; the judgment $t : A \vdash q$ states that if $t$ evaluates to a result of type $A$, then at least $q$ units of resource must be available---that is, $q$ is a lower bound. Because potential makes typing formulas non-replicable, our system follows an affine discipline instead of the replicable contexts of the original framework. We interpret types by semantic typing over value states, pairs of values and remaining resources, and we prove soundness on a safety fragment; corollaries recover the classical two-sided guarantees and the soundness of both kinds of bounds in a single proof system. A prototype type checker in OCaml verifies, on a suite of 19 benchmarks, matching pairs of bounds that characterize costs exactly, as well as lower bounds for programs whose upper bounds are unavailable. In a parallel exploration, we study a two-sided linear type system in which every value is a non-replicable resource; there, closures that capture linear resources call for dual typing formulas, and the exact accounting explains the affine design of the main system.
item.dc:creator: Zimu Chen, Di Wang

item.title: SPMW: A Grid-Based Programming Model for Scalable Accelerator Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.12944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern accelerators specialize recurring computation and replicate it across regular hardware structures to achieve high performance. Sustaining this parallelism requires equally deliberate data delivery. Yet design tools often express these structures as sequential programs or flatten them into separate hardware modules and connections. This obscures shared patterns and leads to repeated compiler work. We introduce Single Program, Multiple Connected Work Units (SPMW), a grid-based programming model for scalable accelerator design that makes grid regularity a first-class abstraction. SPMW decouples local work-unit behavior from grid connectivity and data delivery. To our knowledge, SPMW is the first programming model to retain regularity throughout the compilation process, combining behavioral HLS with structural RTL generation for both fixed-function and domain-specific instruction-programmable accelerators. We implement SPMW with a Python frontend and an MLIR-based compiler that synthesizes each distinct kernel configuration once for reuse across independent hardware instances. Preserving regularity also enables parallel compilation and functional simulation to accelerate iterative design feedback. We use SPMW to generate a 32x32 systolic array that reduces GEMM latency and parallel kernel-to-RTL compilation time by 4.36x and 619x relative to AutoSA. Our FFT achieves up to 2.65x lower latency than HP-FFT. Our mini-TPU and our SPMW implementation of the FEATHER accelerator demonstrate complex composition and outperform their RTL baselines. Parallel functional simulation provides up to 18.4x speedup over Vitis HLS C simulation on the mini-TPU workloads. SPMW is also agent-friendly: given the same design specification, all five coding agents produce SPMW designs that satisfy the correctness and latency requirements, with 7.51x lower token usage than for SystemVerilog.
item.dc:creator: Hongzheng Chen, Shihan Fang, Niansong Zhang, Sunwoo Kim, Weiran Liu, Zhiru Zhang

item.title: Parametric Proof-Carrying Compilation for Quantum Error-Correction
item.description: arXiv:2611.12985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present PC-QEC, a proof-carrying compilation framework for quantum error correction parameterized by both code distance and syndrome-extraction scheme. It covers all four schemes---Standard, Flag, Shor and Knill---with circuit-level distance guarantees for every legal code distance in each proved family under the declared fault and readout contracts. The circuit-level model permits single-wire Pauli faults at every operation's qubit operands, capturing data errors, readout errors and ancilla faults that propagate into multi-qubit hook errors. For each family and scheme, code-algebra proofs and fault-aware Hoare proofs compose into a finite symbolic certificate whose size is independent of code distance. We demonstrate family-wide guarantees for five code families across all four schemes. For rotated Surface code, one Standard Scheme certificate proves a distance lower bound $d$ for every odd $d\ge3$ and checks in 214\,s on average. Lean 4 mechanizes the metatheory and exact circuit-level distances for canonical Surface, hypergraph-product (HGP) and Toric code families.
item.dc:creator: John Zhuoyang Ye, Jens Palsberg

item.title: Context Types: Bunched Modalities for Unifying Safety and Reachability
item.description: arXiv:2611.13471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most type systems are designed to verify safety properties: the judgement $e : \tau$ holds if $e$ may evaluate to any value contained in the denotation of $\tau$, but nothing more. More recent type systems have considered the complementary class of reachability properties: in these systems, the typing judgment holds if $e$ must be able to evaluate to every value denoted by $\tau$, and possibly more. This paper introduces a refinement type system for higher-order functional programs where types can capture both safety and reachability properties. Simultaneously supporting both is challenging because each imposes different constraints on how variable bindings in a typing context are interpreted. We address this challenge by treating typing contexts as a kind of resource that mediates which capabilities are available when typing a program. We formalize this notion by developing a resource algebra of contextual capabilities and a bunched modal context logic over this algebra. We then interpret our type system in this logic, establishing soundness with respect to a denotational semantics that unifies safety and reachability guarantees within a single typing judgement.
item.dc:creator: Zhe Zhou, Benjamin Delaware, Suresh Jagannathan

item.title: Curriculum proof repair with learned counterexamples
item.description: arXiv:2611.13627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models (LMs) have substantially lowered the barrier to applying formal verification for building reliable and secure software. Existing approaches commonly follow the verifier-in-the-loop paradigm, but the verifier often provides only coarse, binary pass/fail feedback, which offers little actionable signal on how the proof should be repaired. Recent work shows that counterexamples provide more actionable feedback by grounding proof failures in concrete program states, but generating useful ones at inference time requires costly iterative refinement. We present TopoVerus, an LM-based framework for Verus proof repair that internalizes counterexample-guided diagnosis as a model capability, producing useful counterexamples in a single pass. Our key insight is to train counterexample generation not as a standalone validation task, but as a data-driven diagnostic objective: a counterexample is useful when conditioning on it helps the model produce a safe, verifier-passing proof. Given a failed Verus proof and verifier error, TopoVerus generates a structured source-level counterexample, repair rationale, and repaired proof in one trajectory, optimized with reinforcement learning from Verus feedback and a proof-code safety gate. To guide the order of invariant repairs, TopoVerus introduces a curriculum with a topological graph reward based on invariant dependencies derived from inductiveness tests, which encourages counterexample generation to follow the same topological order. Across seven Verus benchmarks with 471 problems, TopoVerus achieves 61.6%/72.2% weighted-average Safe-Pass@1/Safe-Pass@3, outperforming the strongest baseline, Claude Sonnet 4.5, by 5.7/6.3 points. We also show that TopoVerus's learned counterexamples can directly augment the reasoning of existing LM-based proof repair approaches, improving their success rate by 64.3% compared to chain-of-thought diagnostics.
item.dc:creator: Yuechun Sun, Jun Yang, Kexin Pei

item.title: Retargetable Compilation for Tensor Kernels via a Unified Layout Abstraction
item.description: arXiv:2611.13741v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern hardware accelerators achieve high performance through specialized instructions coupled with tightly managed memory hierarchies. These instructions impose strict layout requirements on their operands: where tensor fragments reside, how they are organized, and how parallel units access them. Such instruction-visible layout is critical to kernel performance, as it determines whether instructions execute correctly and how much data movement they incur. However, existing compilers either scatter layout requirements across handwritten programs and local scheduling rules, or provide layout representations and conversions specific to a single class of targets. Both approaches expose the same abstraction gap: the absence of a unified model for instruction layout requirements across backends. This paper presents Arknife, a retargetable compiler that treats instruction-visible layout as first-class instruction semantics. Its central idea is a constraint-based layout algebra: tensor layouts map logical axes to hardware axes spanning parallel levels and memory spaces. Instruction operands declare layout requirements, and target-provided repairs resolve conflicts. Layouts are then solved globally across the program. ISA-specific layout facts are supplied by target-side instruction descriptions rather than hardcoded in the compiler. Retargeting reuses the layout algebra and solver while defining the new target's instructions and their operand requirements. We evaluate Arknife across x86 CPU, Hexagon NPU, and NVIDIA A100 GPU. Arknife matches cuBLAS on A100, and on x86 and Hexagon outperforms vendor-optimized libraries by $2.17\times$ and $3.78\times$ and the retargetable compiler MISAAL by $5.08\times$ and $4.53\times$, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Likai Ma, Renze Chen, Tianqi Li, Yuhao Luo, Youwei Xiao, Size Zheng, Xiuhong Li, Yun Liang

item.title: CFGKAT: A Complete Calculus for Non-Local Control Flow
item.description: arXiv:2611.14201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: CFGKAT is an extension of guarded Kleene Algebra with Tests (GKAT) that adds non-local control flow (e.g., break, goto) while maintaining an efficient decision procedure. An axiomatization of equivalence for CFGKAT presents unique barriers created by the presence of non-local control flow and contextual semantics of goto which compromises compositional reasoning. In this paper, we overcome these barriers and present a sound and complete axiomatization of program equivalence in CFGKAT. We verify the loop case of the Erosa-Hendren goto elimination algorithm, a difficult syntactic metatheorem which requires reasoning about fixpoints, control-flow contexts, and mutable state. We mechanize the metatheory and case study in Rocq.
item.dc:creator: Spencer Van Koevering, Alexandra Silva, Cheng Zhang, Tobias Kapp\'e

item.title: Efficient Conversion of Algorithms to Linear Programs
item.description: arXiv:2611.12896v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The expressiveness of Linear Programming (LP) has motivated research on an LP compiler that generates polynomial-size LPs for polynomial-time solvable problems, including those having exponential extension complexity. By automating modeling from high-level algorithmic descriptions, the compiler offers a promising alternative to algebraic modelling languages. However, the resulting LPs are extremely large, posing challenges for existing solvers. Recently, we have introduced two LP compiler optimizations, namely Hierarachical Synchronization Barriers (HSB) and Constraint Sharing (CS), that address this challenge by exploiting structural and similarity-based patterns derived from the source code and the design of compiler-generated LPs, beyond what conventional compiler and presolve techniques can achieve in isolation. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive evaluation of these optimization methods on fundamental combinatorial algorithms and introduce the Execution Domain Aware (EDA) optimization framework to address a limitation revealed by this analysis. The framework reinterprets structural synchronizations as a time abstraction layer within which other optimizations can target localized reductions while remaining agnostic to time-step transitions. Across a broad suite of benchmarks, HSB and CS consistently generate smaller LPs, achieving LP file-size reductions of up to 96% and 53%, respectively, while also improving numerical conditioning, solver performance, and solution quality. HSB provides the strongest and most robust overall gains. The EDA framework further broadens the range of benchmarks that can benefit from HSB when its underlying structural assumptions are less effective. We view this work as a step toward systematic generation of Compact Integer Programming formulations for problems with exponential-size Integer Programs having polynomial-time separation oracles.
item.dc:creator: Shermin Khosravi, David Bremner

item.title: The Left Ripple of Byte-Pair Encoding: Certified Lookbehind for Every Dictionary
item.description: arXiv:2611.13061v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Berglund and van der Merwe formalized byte-pair encoding and bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization, leaving the converse open: how far can a string prepended on the left change it, which dictionaries make that ripple infinite, and can it be computed efficiently when finite? We answer all three for every dictionary. The origin radius, how far a prepend can change covering spans, is decided with radius certificates by a product of two runs of the automaton that guesses the final tokens, in time polynomial in the dictionary written out, and it is infinite exactly when one periodic word has two canonical tilings with no common boundary. Under their ordering condition it is infinite exactly when some rule (t, t) finds its two copies adjacent at its own stage, and such a rule makes any dictionary infinite. A finite radius makes every window of a width read off the radii have a cut, and the radius is finite exactly when such cuts are dense. The token machine completes for every dictionary, and the tokenization is subsequential, extending what Berglund, Martens and van der Merwe proved for proper ones under one pass per rule. A streaming tokenizer emits after every symbol exactly the tokens that no continuation changes, in polynomial time, answering a question of Dalirrooyfard and Ye. Boundedness of the label measure, the edit distance of the token sequences, is decided for every dictionary in polynomial time as well, and under the ordering condition the largest distance one edit causes over dictionaries of m rules lies asymptotically between m^2/10 and m^2/2. GPT-2's merge table carries 244 effective self-pairs, so its origin radius is infinite from the forty-second merge on, and that of cl100k, o200k and Llama 3 from their first. Every measured number is its program's output, and what is not executed is named.
item.dc:creator: Nicklas Nidh\"ogg

item.title: G\"odel's Incompleteness Theorems in Grounded Arithmetic
item.description: arXiv:2611.13697v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) is a paracomplete arithmetic in which every term is a program and truth is grounded evaluation. RGA discharges a hypothesis only when it proves the hypothesis decided. This paper shows, in a machine-checked Isabelle/HOL development, how G\"odel's incompleteness theorems hold for RGA and for systems built on it. RGA's implication is material and RGA has the disjunction property, so the implications the textbook proof of the second theorem uses fail while its entailments and rules hold: G\"odel's proof survives as entailments. RGA does not prove its consistency sentence Con, and RGA derives its own second theorem as the entailment $\mathit{Con}\vdash\neg\mathit{Pr}(\ulcorner\mathit{Con}\urcorner)$ and as one sentence quantified over proofs. The second theorem is then proved once, for every G\"odel extension of RGA: an entailment relation on RGA's language, closed under RGA's rules, with a checker that meets three structural conditions, NEC, D3 and EXPL as proof transformers, D1 as closed acceptance, and consistency. D2 is not among the conditions. RGA with its checker is one instance. Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA), RGA with ground induction, is another, its checker adding one rule detector, and IGA does not derive its consistency sentence for it. Adoption, a reflection rule whose premise is a derived warrant that the checker accepts computed proofs of every instance of a universal, gives consistent extensions RGA$^+$ and IGA$^+$. RGA$^+$ derives RGA's consistency sentence and IGA$^+$ derives RGA's and IGA's, so each strictly extends its base, and IGA$^+$ both. The second theorem holds at every adopted notation claim, and adopting Turing's code for that claim's checker derives its consistency sentence, so no claim certifies itself. Whether IGA alone derives RGA's consistency sentence is open, and the paper names what two routes to an answer need.
item.dc:creator: Bryan Ford

item.title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
item.description: arXiv:2611.14147v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent. To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.
item.dc:creator: Zhicheng Zhang, Mingsheng Ying, Lirong Xia

item.title: Performance Portability Explained: Insights from accelerating ICON microphysics
item.description: arXiv:2611.14204v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scientific computing is under increasing pressure to adapt to HPC hardware that is shaped by AI workloads. In these modern ecosystems, extracting reasonable performance without investing major engineering effort is a central issue for domain scientists. Correctness constraints and intricate reference implementations represent further impediments to development. Instead of using a double-precision implementation as a reference, considering the underlying scientific problem directly opens more opportunities for performance improvements when updating and rewriting applications. We take seven different portability frameworks---covering pragma-based, DSL, and data-centric approaches---and evaluate them on a microphysics kernel of the ICON climate model. Our performance benchmarks show that each different HPC system benefits from a different combination of optimizations, so we develop the measure of framework expressivity to gauge how easily each framework can customize portable implementations in this way.
item.dc:creator: Faveo H\"orold, Georgiana Mania, Panagiotis Adamidis, Harshada Balasubramanian, J\"org Behrens, Yakup Budanaz, Alexandru Calotoiu, Nicoletta Farabullini, Andreas Herten, Torsten Hoefler, Yannik Koenneker, Ioannis Magkanaris, Philip M\"uller, Ralf M\"uller, Edoardo Paone, William Sawyer, Bjorn Stevens, Hannes Vogt

item.title: For Generalised Algebraic Theories, Two Sorts Are Enough
item.description: arXiv:2601.19426v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generalised algebraic theories (GATs) allow multiple sorts indexed over each other. Categories have two sorts, objects and morphisms, and the latter are double-indexed over the former. Martin-L\"of type theory has four sorts: contexts, substitutions, types and terms. For example, types are indexed over contexts, and terms are indexed over both contexts and types. In this paper we show that any GAT can be reduced to a GAT involving only two sorts: a first one without dependencies, and another one indexed over the former. We show that a model of the reduced GAT is equivalently given by a pair consisting of a model of the original GAT, which we call the core model, and a "cartesian" morphism from the family of sets induced by this core model. In a type-theoretic metatheory, the initial model of a GAT is called a quotient inductive-inductive type (QIIT). The above characterisation justifies soundness of the reduction, in the sense that the QIIT of the original GAT can be simulated from the QIIT of the reduced GAT, by taking its core model. A particular case of our reduction is the well-known method of reducing mutual inductive types to a single indexed family. Other instances of this reduction can be found in the literature to simulate sophisticated QIITs in Cubical Agda. Indeed, the reduced GAT is simpler than the original GAT in the following aspects: it does not have sort equalities; it does not have interleaved sorts and operations; if the original GAT did not have interleaved sorts and operations, then the reduced GAT won't have operations interleaved between different sorts. Our approach is semantic in that it does not rely on a syntactic description of GATs, but instead, on Uemura's bi-initial characterisation of the category of (finite) GATs in the 2-category of finitely complete categories with a chosen exponentiable morphism.
item.dc:creator: Samy Avrillon, Ambrus Kaposi, Ambroise Lafont, Niyousha Najmaei, Johann Rosain

item.title: RECURSUM: Automated Code Generation for Recurrence Relations Exceeds Expert Optimization via LayeredCodegen
item.description: arXiv:2604.18585v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automated code generation can systematically exceed expert hand-optimization for recurrence relations--computational primitives ubiquitous in orthogonal polynomials, special functions, numerical integration, and molecular integral evaluation. We present RECURSUM, a Python DSL generating optimized C++ for arbitrary recurrence relations via three backends--template metaprogramming, a novel LayeredCodegen backend, and runtime loop-based evaluation--specifying recurrences in 10--30 lines of Python that generate 650+ lines of production C++. LayeredCodegen achieves 9.8$\times$ speedup over expert hand-written code and 1.9$\times$ over template metaprogramming for McMurchie-Davidson Hermite coefficients, through zero-copy output parameters, guaranteed inlining, and exact-sized stack buffers. A DAG-topological generalization of this architecture--built to express the four-center electron-repulsion integral that LayeredCodegen's tower model cannot--beats libint2, a mature, two-decade-refined production library, on 12 of 14 Cartesian integral classes, with $\sim$2$\times$ faster contracted Coulomb/exchange (J/K) matrix construction (alkanes and 3-D DNA fragments alike) and 1.1--2.7$\times$ faster one-electron integrals, completing the full Hartree-Fock integral set from one DAG framework. We validate 24 recurrence types spanning pure mathematics, numerical analysis, and quantum chemistry; production benchmarks confirm these speedups propagate to complete algorithms, matching expert baselines within 3.3\%. By eliminating the dual expertise barrier of domain knowledge and C++ metaprogramming, RECURSUM establishes systematic code generation--not hand-tuning--as the performance ceiling for recurrence algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Rub\'en Dar\'io Guerrero

item.title: Fibered Separation Logic: Weakest Preconditions, Universal Constructions, and Local Independence
item.description: arXiv:2611.08685v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper introduces a categorical framework for models of higher-order separation logic including the weakest precondition modality. Weakest preconditions are interpreted by strong monads on a category fibered over a model of Moggi's computational lambda calculus. The fibered categories in question are termed bunched fibrations and shown to be equivalent to BI hyperdoctrines. Well-known heuristic techniques for obtaining weakest preconditions are shown to be expressible in categorical terms and are proved sound. The ``baking in the frame rule'' trick is shown to satisfy a universal property. Constructions are given for extending a program logic with cost credits. Our largest case study is parametrized by a category having local independent product (LIP) structure, a notion due to Simpson that axiomatizes name generation, randomness, and local state. From an LIP category, we construct an allocation monad, a bunched fibration, and a monad lifting. We instantiate our construction to obtain a novel probabilistic separation logic for measure-theoretic probability that both simplifies and clarifies prior work.
item.dc:creator: John M. Li, Ryan Doenges, Pedro H. Azevedo de Amorim
